title: Using your portfolio & reflective accounts
blurb: How your Portfolio of Evidence works, which evidence counts, how to write reflections that show insight, and how to turn it all into discussion examples.
question: Your Professional Discussion is in three weeks. Your portfolio holds dozens of entries: witness testimonies, photos of set-ups, reflective accounts. How do you turn that into ready examples for each of the nine duties, and what makes a reflection worth talking about?

teach.h: Your portfolio is your raw material
teach.body: NEBDN says the Professional Discussion is based on knowledge and practical activities completed in the workplace that relate to the nine duties. Your Portfolio of Evidence is the record of exactly those activities. Every witness testimony, observation and reflection is a ready-made example you can talk about. Learners who know their portfolio well walk in with real stories; learners who don't are left trying to remember on the spot.

The portfolio is completed digitally on PebblePad while you are on programme, and must be assessed over a minimum of six months. It is assessed by your provider and internally quality assured, and NEBDN samples portfolios through external quality assurance. It is graded pass or fail and must be passed before the Professional Discussion. All work must be your own: copied work is not accepted and can be treated as malpractice.

head: Type
Example
rows: Written or audio account of work done
A registrant who watched you work
Your assessor sees you in practice
e.g. setting up for a procedure
teach.caption: Some assessment criteria require a mandatory witness testimony. NEBDN says the list is not exhaustive.

teach.text: No patient-identifiable information or images go in your portfolio unless the patient has given written consent. When you talk about a patient in the discussion, keep it anonymous too: "a patient in her seventies", never a name.

teach.h: Map at least one example to each duty
teach.caption: Examples only: use your own. Aim for two per duty so you have a back-up.

teach.body: A reflective account is where you show insight: that you understand what you did, why it mattered, where your limits were and how you've grown. Insight matters because it is how you keep patients safe and keep developing. A strong reflection is honest (including about mistakes), specific, analyses why things happened, links to standards or guidance, and ends with a clear change in your practice.

teach.caption: What happened? So what does it mean: why did it matter, what did I learn, which standard applies? Now what will I do differently, and how will I check it worked?

teach.h: Build your evidence bank before the day
items: List the nine duties and note two portfolio examples under each.
For each example, jot down: what you did, why, which standard or guidance applies, and what you learned.
Reread your reflective accounts so the details are fresh.
Check every example stays within the dental nurse's scope.
Practise telling each example aloud in about two minutes.
The discussion draws on workplace activities, so your portfolio is your best source of examples.
PebblePad, at least six months, provider-assessed, NEBDN quality assured, pass or fail.
Accepted evidence includes work products, witness testimony, observation, video, records and feedback.
No patient-identifiable information without written consent, in the portfolio or the discussion.
Strong reflections show insight: analysis, honesty, links to standards and a real change.

summary: You can now explain how the Portfolio of Evidence is built and assessed, name the evidence NEBDN accepts, keep patient information confidential, write reflective accounts that show insight using What? So what? Now what?, and turn your portfolio into a bank of examples for every duty.

A.q: Over what minimum period must the NEBDN Portfolio of Evidence be assessed?
options: Three months
Twelve months
Eighteen months
Six months
A.why: NEBDN's specification says the portfolio must be assessed over a minimum of six months.

whyNot.0: Three months is shorter than the six-month minimum.
whyNot.1: Twelve months is not the minimum set by NEBDN.
whyNot.2: Eighteen months is the typical length of the apprenticeship standard, not the portfolio minimum.

A.q: You want to include a clinical photo of a patient's teeth in your portfolio. What does NEBDN require?
options: The dentist's verbal permission
The patient's written consent
Nothing, as teeth can't identify anyone
Blurring the photo before uploading it
A.why: No patient-identifiable information or images may be included unless the patient has given written consent.

whyNot.0: It is the patient's consent that matters, and it must be written.
whyNot.2: Clinical images can identify patients; consent is still needed.
whyNot.3: Blurring isn't the NEBDN requirement; written patient consent is.

A.q: In Driscoll's "What? So what? Now what?" model, what does the "So what?" stage explore?
options: What the situation means and what you learned
A factual account of exactly what happened
The date, the time and the people who were present
Your plan for what to do next time
A.why: "So what?" is the analysis: why it mattered, what you learned and which standards apply.

whyNot.1: A factual account is the "What?" stage.
whyNot.2: These details belong to the description, the "What?" stage.
whyNot.3: Your plan for next time is the "Now what?" stage.

B.q: Who assesses the Portfolio of Evidence?
options: Your provider, with NEBDN quality assurance
The GDC, at the point you apply to register
Your employing dentist, working alone
An NEBDN examiner during the discussion
B.why: The portfolio is assessed and internally quality assured by your provider, and NEBDN samples it through external quality assurance.

whyNot.1: The GDC doesn't assess NEBDN portfolios.
whyNot.2: Your dentist may act as a witness, but doesn't assess the portfolio alone.
whyNot.3: The portfolio must be passed before the discussion, not marked during it.

B.q: Which reflective account shows the most insight?
options: "The clinic was very busy that day, but it all went fine in the end."
"The dentist was rushing, so the mistake was really hers."
"I wasn't sure of the steps, so I asked, then booked training."
"I learned a lot and will try to do better next time."
B.why: Recognising a limit, asking for help and taking specific action to develop is exactly what insight looks like.

whyNot.0: This is description only, with no learning.
whyNot.1: Blaming others shows little insight into your own part.
whyNot.3: This is vague; there is no analysis or specific change.

B.q: Which of these is NOT acceptable portfolio evidence?
options: A witness testimony from a registered colleague
Feedback from a patient about your care
A reflection copied from another learner
A video of you setting up for a procedure
B.why: All work must be your own. Copied work is not accepted and can be treated as malpractice.

whyNot.0: Witness testimony is an accepted form of evidence.
whyNot.1: Feedback from colleagues or patients is accepted.

C.q: Who can provide a witness testimony for your portfolio?
options: A friend who visited the practice once to watch
A GDC registrant who observed you directly
Any patient you helped to treat that week
A receptionist at your practice
C.why: Witnesses must hold GDC registration with competence in the area, and directly observe you. NEBDN recommends they have worked with you on two prior occasions.

whyNot.0: A visitor isn't a registered professional and hasn't properly observed your competence.
whyNot.2: Patient feedback is a different type of evidence, not a witness testimony.
whyNot.3: Witnesses must be GDC registrants with competence in the area.

C.q: Three weeks before the discussion, what is the best way to use your portfolio?
options: Pick two examples per duty and rehearse them
Memorise model answers you found online
Reread only the unit you found hardest
Leave it alone, as it has already been passed
C.why: Choosing real examples for each duty and rehearsing what you did, why and what you learned prepares you for any duty the assessor explores.

whyNot.1: Model answers aren't your own experience, and NEBDN doesn't publish the questions.
whyNot.2: The discussion covers all nine duties, not one unit.
whyNot.3: The discussion draws on your workplace activities, so the portfolio is your best preparation.

C.q: In Driscoll's model, which question does the "Now what?" stage answer?
options: Who else was involved?
How did I feel at the time?
Why did it matter?
What will I do differently?
C.why: "Now what?" turns learning into action: what you'll change and how you'll check it worked.

whyNot.0: Who was involved is part of describing what happened.
whyNot.1: Feelings are part of describing and exploring the experience.
whyNot.2: Why it mattered is the "So what?" stage.

reteach.title: Your portfolio is a photo album
reteach.question: If your portfolio were an album of photos from training, how would you use it to tell your story?

blocks.body: Each piece of evidence is a snapshot: a moment from your training. On its own a photo just shows what happened. The caption is your reflection: why that moment mattered and what you changed afterwards. In the discussion you are flicking through the album with the assessor, choosing the right photo for each duty and telling the story behind it, without showing anyone's face unless they agreed.

steps.label: Caption
steps.sub: Why it mattered; the standard behind it

blocks.text: An album of photos with no captions tells the assessor very little. Evidence without reflection shows what you did, but not that you understand it.

explain.body: Built on PebblePad over at least six months. Assessed by your provider, internally quality assured and sampled by NEBDN. Pass or fail, and passed before the discussion.

test.q: On which platform is the NEBDN Portfolio of Evidence completed?
options: MaxExam
PebblePad
TheHub
eGDC
test.why: NEBDN's specification says the portfolio is completed digitally on PebblePad.

whyNot.0: MaxExam is used for the Knowledge Test.
whyNot.2: TheHub is NEBDN's system for providers to manage learners.
whyNot.3: eGDC is the GDC's registrant portal.

explain.body: Work products, personal statements, witness testimonies, assessor observations, videos, training and appraisal records, and feedback from colleagues or patients.

test.q: A colleague writes a signed account of watching you mix and pass materials during a filling. What type of evidence is this?
options: Personal statement
Work product
Assessor observation
Witness testimony
test.why: A registrant directly observing you and testifying to your competence is a witness testimony.

whyNot.0: A personal statement is written by you about your own work.
whyNot.1: Work products are items like photos, documents or reports.
whyNot.2: An assessor observation is carried out by your assessor.

explain.body: No patient-identifiable information or images without the patient's written consent. In the discussion, describe patients anonymously.

test.q: In the discussion, how should you refer to a patient from one of your examples?
options: By their first name only, to keep it friendly
By their initials and age
Anonymously, e.g. "an elderly patient"
By the date and time of their appointment
test.why: Describing patients anonymously protects confidentiality while still letting you explain the situation.

whyNot.0: A first name can help identify a patient.
whyNot.1: Initials with an age can still identify someone.
whyNot.3: An appointment date can identify a patient when combined with other details.

explain.body: What? So what? Now what? Describe it, analyse what it means and what you learned, then say what you'll do differently.

test.q: Which ending best completes a strong reflective account?
options: "I now check the history with every patient before they sit down."
"Overall, looking back, I felt that it all went quite well in the end."
"It was a really busy day in clinic, so these things do happen."
"Next time, hopefully, it will go a lot better for everyone."
test.why: A strong reflection ends with a specific change in practice, the "Now what?".

whyNot.1: This is a feeling, not a change in practice.
whyNot.2: This excuses the event rather than learning from it.
whyNot.3: This is vague, with no specific action.
